lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rafael Pelizaro | Lesson 23 -- Sharing the Workload
lesson.grammar_point: have to / don't have to / mustn't (obligation, no obligation, prohibition)

listenings.text: I lead a support team of eight people, and my most important job is to protect their capacity. When the workload is too high, people work overtime, and after a month they start to make mistakes. So we have three simple rules. First, nobody has to be on call two weeks in a row. We change every Monday. Second, our weekly meeting is optional for anyone with nothing new to say. You don't have to come; you just have to write two lines in the chat. Third, and this one is mandatory: you mustn't say yes to a new request without checking your bandwidth first. A tired team doesn't need more meetings. It needs fewer tasks and clear limits.

For years, I had a problem: I didn't know how to delegate. I used to think that a good manager has to know everything and do the difficult tasks himself. So I worked overtime almost every night, and my team waited for me. Then my director asked me a simple question: which tasks do you really have to do yourself? The honest answer was: very few. I made a list. Approving the budget, talking to the board and hiring are mine. Everything else, I don't have to do. Now each engineer owns one area, and I only check the results on Friday. My team is faster, and I go home at six. The lesson was clear: if you never delegate, you become the bottleneck.
